prompt: Both nodes are assembled, powered and healthy. You press the USER button on either one and neither LINK LED lights. What does the pair still need?
options: One board flashed as sender, one as receiver: identical hardware leaves the role to firmware
The expansion-header jumper that picks which of the two boards transmits
A wire between the two headers, since ESP-NOW peers need a shared reference

prompt: The expansion header brings out ADC1 pins and no ADC2 pins at all. What drives that choice on this board in particular?
options: The ADC2 pins are already committed to the module's native USB data pair
ADC1 inputs tolerate 5 V, which makes them the safe choice on a header
The radio claims ADC2 whenever it runs, and this radio never stops running

prompt: Your cart holds three B3F buttons and every line matched an exact MPN. What is still wrong?
options: Nothing: the board carries three buttons and the BOM lists three
The BOM is per node and you build two, so the cart wants six plus spares
The USER button rides the chip's internal pull-up, so two buttons suffice

prompt: D1, the USBLC6 ESD array, goes out of stock the week you order. What does your BOM line already tell you to do?
options: Leave D1 off: the polyfuse and the CC resistors already guard the port
Fit the second source the line names, the UMW USBLC6-2SC6
Substitute any SOT-23-6 diode array that drops into the same footprint

prompt: You wire SW3's far leg to +3V3 instead of GND. ERC passes clean. What does the finished board do?
options: GPIO21 reads high pressed or not, so every press is invisible
The internal pull-up fights the button and the pin oscillates
The board refuses to boot, since GPIO21 is sampled at reset

prompt: EN and GPIO0 each carry an external 10 kΩ pull-up. GPIO21 carries none. What decides which pins get a real resistor?
options: How much current the switch has to carry when it closes
Whether the pin sits on ADC1 or on the radio-shared ADC2
Whether the level must be defined before any firmware runs

prompt: A learner jumpers the header's 5V position across to one of its GPIO positions, to power a small sensor from there. What happens?
options: Nothing: the pin regulates the 5 V down to 3.3 V on its way in
The sensor browns out, since a GPIO sources only a few milliamps
The pin can be destroyed: ESP32-S3 GPIO are 3.3 V parts

prompt: You drew the antenna rule area, poured ground, and the pour filled straight through it. What did the rule area fail to say?
options: Keep out copper pours, on all four copper layers
Keep out silkscreen, which the pour follows on the outer layers
That the board outline has to stop short of the antenna

prompt: Two finished nodes link reliably at arm's length and drop out across the room. Which layout mistake matches that symptom?
options: The USB pair was drawn trace by trace instead of with the pair router
Copper reached into the keep-out, and a detuned antenna radiates less
The power nets were left on the Default class at 0.25 mm

prompt: The node resets every time it transmits, and the trouble started when you moved the 0.1 µF caps away from U1 to make room. Why does that distance matter?
options: The longer traces add resistance, which drops the rail below 3.0 V
A capacitor loses capacitance the further it sits from the regulator
The loop grows, and its inductance resists the fast current step

prompt: You renamed a net in the schematic, exported Gerbers straight afterwards, and the built board's LINK LED never lights. Which check would have caught it?
options: Test for parity between PCB and schematic, ticked in the DRC run
Refill all zones, so DRC measures the copper you actually export
The Gerber job file, which pins down which file is which layer

prompt: You need two identical nodes. What does the board order look like?
options: Two uploads of the same zip, one order per board you need
One zip at the minimum quantity of 5: two to build, three spare
One zip with panelisation, so both boards arrive on one panel

prompt: The quote offers HASL free and ENIG for a few dollars more. What does ENIG buy on this board?
options: A finish that resists corrosion across the board's service life
Dead-flat pads under the WROOM's fine-pitch castellations
A gold surface that wets at a lower soldering temperature

prompt: Two bare boards, hot iron, flux already out. What is the efficient build order?
options: Finish board A completely, then set the bench up again for board B
Alternate part by part between boards so both progress together
Each pass on both boards while the bench is set for that pass

prompt: Board A passed its VBUS-to-GND continuity sweep. What does board B need before it sees power?
options: Its own sweep: a solder bridge is a per-board accident
Nothing: identical boards give identical results
A visual pass only, since the meter cleared this design

prompt: Why run the whole solo ladder on each board before the first link test?
options: A dead link across two unproven boards means debugging two unknowns
The radio wants several minutes on a settled rail before it transmits
A board only prints its factory MAC after it has enumerated once

prompt: You paste each board's own printed MAC into its own config. Both boards run happily and nothing ever arrives. What went wrong?
options: The two boards ended up pinned to different Wi-Fi channels
Both boards are running receiver firmware, so nobody transmits
Packets carry a destination: each config needs the peer's MAC

prompt: The link ran for five minutes on a USB power bank, then the receiver went dark. What is the documented cause?
options: The PTC fuse tripped and needs time to cool before it resets
The power bank auto-slept under the light load
The radio overheated and the transmitter shut itself down
